newsitem.title: SIERRA LEONE: Foreigners quit Sierra Leone after coup.
newsitem.headline: Foreigners quit Sierra Leone after coup.

text.p: Helicopters shuttled foreigners to Freetown's international airport on Thursday for evacuation following a weekend coup in the West African state, while others headed out by boat.
Sierra Leone's ambassador to Washington urged U.S. Marines on board a helicopter ship off Freetown to support Nigerian troops in restoring the elected government ousted on Sunday.

The helicopter evacuation was hampered by rain and technical problems, but organiser Greg McKinley promised the bedraggled families waiting at a beachside hotel the chartered jumbo jet would stay on the ground until it was full.
The Americans will evacuate U.S. citizens by helicopter to a U.S. Navy ship, the Kearsarge, on Friday and then fly them to Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea.

"It wasn't the welcome I had hoped for," said Canadian George Cone, 42, from Calgary who arrived only last Thursday on his first trip to Africa to organise training for a cellular phone company setting up a network in Sierra Leone.

Trades unions and other civil groups have called on people to stay at home in protest against the coup. City centre streets were deserted apart from a few soldiers whose behaviour was in no way menacing.
An armoured car and an automatic machinegun were set up outside the bullet-pocked presidential offices at State House.

Sierra Leone's ambassador to Washington John Leigh said he wanted the 1,200 Marines aboard the Kearsarge to support West African peace forces "to bring in law and order" and end a "reign of terror" by the coup leaders, whom he described as "wild savages".

Nigeria has sent hundreds of troops to bolster the West African ECOMOG peacekeeping contingent based in Sierra Leone but they were visible only at the two hotels where foreigners awaiting evacuation have taken refuge.

On Wednesday, a helicopter chartered by Belgian carrier Sabena flew 130 people to Conakry, capital of neighbouring Guinea. A Boeing 707 plane sent by Lebanon evacuated 178 Lebanese, most of them women and children. It also carried the bodies of two Lebanese men killed in the coup.
A U.N.-chartered boat carried 97 people to Conakry and was expected to make a second trip on Thursday.

The new military authorities who seized power on Sunday blamed harassment of civilians on former servicemen and escaped prisoners in army uniform and warned they would be arrested, apparently oblivious to the fact that the most prominent escaped prisoner was new head of state, Major Johnny Paul Koromah.

Koromah, 33, was among those freed from Freetown's Pademba Road prison early on Sunday at the start of the coup. He was detained on treason charges over an earlier alleged coup attempt against civilian president Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, who flew to Guinea on Sunday.

Koromah's Armed Forces Revolutionary Council (AFRC) set up hotlines for the public to complain about harassment and looting, though it was unlikely many people would risk reporting looting which witnesses say is carried out mainly by soldiers.
"The AFRC is appealing to all Sierra Leoneans to cooperate with the Army to restore peace, law, and order in our beloved country," a statement said. "Your complaints will be thoroughly investigated."

West African military sources acknowledged that a steady buildup of Nigerian troops was part of a regional plan to reinstate Kabbah. No military move was expected until the evacuations were completed, the sources said.
"Major Johnny Paul Koromah and his comrades should consider the party over and negotiate their return to the barracks," said a commentary on Nigerian state radio.
"It will be the wisest thing to do, because ECOWAS wants the military quickly out of politics, and because Nigeria shares this resolve."
